47413:
In the first-century world, life was organised around the household (*oikos*): an extended family with slaves, workers, clients and guests, often running a business from home. Churches met in households (Rom 16:5, Col 4:15), and whole households were baptised (Acts 16:15, Acts 16:33). Ministry therefore looked less like a programme run from a building and more like a family's shared life: meals, hospitality, teaching at table, caring for members' needs. Paul calls the church "the household of God" (1 Tim 3:15) and requires elders to manage their own households well.

Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in Jewish tradition, modelled by Abraham at Mamre (Gen 18:1-8; see Heb 13:2). Travelling apostles, prophets and teachers depended on it, which is why 3 John praises Gaius for supporting them and the Didache tells churches how to test them. The Greek *philoxenia* means "love of strangers".

Patronage was the social glue of the Roman world. Wealthy patrons provided protection, money and status; clients repaid them with loyalty and public honour. The gospel both used and transformed this system. Women and men of means, such as Joanna, Susanna, Lydia and Phoebe, used their resources for Christ's mission (Luke 8:1-3, Rom 16:1-2). But Jesus warns against seeking honour by giving and tells hosts to invite those who cannot repay (Luke 14:12-14). God is the ultimate patron whose grace (*charis*) creates a relationship of gratitude and loyalty, and believers become patrons for one another (David deSilva, *Honor, Patronage, Kinship and Purity*, 2000).

Seen this way, many ministries modern churches overlook were central: opening one's home, using wealth and influence for others, raising children in the faith, caring for widows and orphans, and welcoming strangers. These were the everyday channels through which the gospel spread.
47415: The pastor is the minister. Church members support the ministry by attending, giving and volunteering for programmes, but real ministry, such as preaching, counselling and visiting, is the pastor's job and what we pay him or her for.
47416: Ephesians 4:11-12 says Christ gives leaders "to equip the saints for the work of ministry". The ministry belongs to the saints; leaders equip. Every believer has a gift for others (1 Pet 4:10), and the body grows "when each part is working properly" (Eph 4:16). Ray Stedman, R. Paul Stevens and Greg Ogden (*Unfinished Business*) argue that the New Testament knows only one people of God, all ministers, some of whom are leaders. Catholic teaching since Vatican II says the same in its own terms: lay people have their own apostolate by baptism.
47417: Defenders of a strong pastoral office, such as many Reformed and Lutheran writers, agree that every believer serves but warn against flattening real distinctions. Scripture does set apart some for preaching and oversight, tells churches to honour and pay them (1 Tim 5:17-18) and to obey their leaders (Heb 13:17). Some also note a grammatical debate in Eph 4:12 about whether leaders both equip and do ministry themselves. The best of both sides agree: leaders have a real and weighty calling, and that calling is to multiply ministry, not monopolise it.
47418: If ministry belongs only to pastors, most gifts lie unused, pastors burn out, and members see themselves as consumers. If every member serves and leaders equip, the church becomes the body Paul describes.
47419: "Secular work is second-class; full-time ministry is the higher calling"
47420: The most committed Christians go into "full-time ministry" as pastors or missionaries. Other jobs are mainly a way to earn money, support the church and find people to evangelise.
47421: Scripture starts with work as worship (Gen 2:15) and tells believers to work "as for the Lord" (Col 3:23-24). Bezalel's craft is Spirit-filled (Exod 31:3), and Joseph, Daniel and Nehemiah serve God in government. Luther attacked the medieval idea of a higher religious estate, teaching that every calling is holy when done in faith. Writers such as Tim Keller, Miroslav Volf and R. Paul Stevens develop a theology of vocation where work itself, not only the witness done at work, matters to God.
47422: Traditional evangelical and missions voices respond that Scripture does call some to leave their nets (Mark 1:16-20) and does tell churches to support gospel workers (1 Cor 9:14). Evangelism and church planting have eternal stakes. Most agree that "full-time" is a misleading phrase, since every Christian is a full-time disciple, but they insist the unique task of gospel proclamation must not be lost in a general theology of work.
47423: Most believers will never be paid by a church. If their work is second-class, they live with guilt or division between Sunday and Monday. If work is ministry, every job becomes a place to serve God and neighbour.
47424: "The priesthood of all believers means I do not need a church or leaders"
47425: Since every believer is a priest with direct access to God, I can interpret Scripture for myself, worship God alone and do not need pastors, sacraments or church authority.
47426: 1 Peter 2:9 is addressed to a people in the plural: "you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood". It echoes Exodus 19:6, where the whole nation is called to be priests for the world. The emphasis is corporate and outward: declaring God's praises to others. Luther used it to argue that all believers can serve and pray for one another, not that each is self-sufficient. Timothy George and other Reformation historians note that Luther spoke of the priesthood of all believers, not the priesthood of each believer alone.
47427: Defenders of individual access, especially in Baptist and free-church tradition, rightly stress that every believer can approach God through Christ without a human mediator (Heb 4:16, 1 Tim 2:5) and must read Scripture for themselves, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). But they also hold that believers belong to local churches with leaders and discipline (Heb 10:24-25, Matt 18:15-17). Catholic and Orthodox theologians add that the common priesthood is real but works together with the ordained priesthood. All agree the doctrine does not license isolation.
47428: Read individualistically, the doctrine can dissolve community and accountability. Read as Scripture means it, it makes every believer a servant who brings others to God and God's praise to others.
47429: "Ephesians 4:11 lists five offices every church must install"
47430: God has given five offices, apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, and a church is incomplete without all five functioning as recognised leaders with authority.
47431: Ephesians 4:11 lists gifted people Christ gives to the church, but the emphasis is on their purpose: equipping all believers for ministry until the body reaches maturity (Eph 4:12-13). The Greek links "shepherds and teachers" closely, so many read four groups. Paul's other lists (Rom 12:6-8, 1 Cor 12:28) differ, suggesting he is not giving a fixed organisational chart. Many continuationists, such as Gordon Fee and Craig Keener, accept ongoing apostolic and prophetic ministry but not a five-office template.
47432: Supporters of fivefold ministry, such as C. Peter Wagner and some Pentecostal networks, argue that Eph 4:13 says these gifts continue "until we all attain to the unity of the faith", which has not yet happened, so all five should remain. Alan Hirsch argues that churches lacking apostolic and prophetic gifts become inward-looking. Cessationists respond that apostles and prophets were foundational (Eph 2:20). Both cessationist and moderate continuationist scholars caution against making the list into a hierarchy.
47433: If the list is a mandatory structure, churches may elevate individuals with titles and little accountability. If it is a description of gifts that equip, every church can ask whether pioneering, prophetic, evangelistic, pastoral and teaching gifts are being encouraged without inventing new hierarchies.
47434: "Phoebe and other women were only helpers"
47435: Women in the New Testament served behind the scenes: making meals, providing money and helping the men who did the real ministry. Phoebe was a "servant" (as older translations say) who helped Paul.
47436: Phoebe is called a diakonos "of the church at Cenchreae", the same word Paul uses for himself and Timothy, and a prostatis, patron, of many including Paul (Rom 16:1-2). She probably carried and presented Romans. Junia is "outstanding among the apostles" (Rom 16:7), Priscilla teaches Apollos (Acts 18:26), and Euodia and Syntyche "contended at my side in the gospel" (Phil 4:2-3). Lynn Cohick, Richard Bauckham and Beverly Gaventa show that women had real influence as patrons and leaders in the early church.
47437: Complementarian scholars such as Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo accept that Phoebe was probably a deacon and a patron, that Priscilla taught, and that women served widely and visibly. They argue that none of these roles is elder oversight, and that "helper" was never meant to diminish. Many now prefer translations like "deacon" or "minister" for Phoebe. The disagreement is about church office, not about whether these women were significant.
47438: Underestimating these women hides real models of courageous service. Overstating the evidence can claim more than the text says. Careful reading honours both the women and the text.
47439: "Jesus abolished teachers, and the scribes were dry legalists"
47440: Jesus said "call no one rabbi" and opposed the scribes and Pharisees, who taught dead rules. So Christianity is about the Spirit, not trained teachers or careful study.
47441: Jesus was himself called Rabbi and taught in synagogues as a Jewish teacher. In Matthew 23:8-12 he warns against loving titles and status, not against teaching, and he commissions his disciples to teach (Matt 28:20). He praises the scribe "trained for the kingdom" who brings out treasures new and old (Matt 13:52). Scholars such as E. P. Sanders and Amy-Jill Levine show that the scribes and Pharisees were respected lay teachers who sought to apply Torah to daily life; Jesus' criticisms target hypocrisy and burden-laying, as other Jewish teachers also did.
47442: Traditional scholars such as D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg agree that "legalists" is a caricature and that Jesus' critique is aimed at specific failures, while noting that the Gospels do record serious conflict over Jesus' authority and the Sabbath. Teaching remains a gift and office in the church (1 Cor 12:28, Jas 3:1), and Ezra the scribe is a model of devotion to the word.
47443: Despising study and teaching weakens the church and repeats an old anti-Jewish caricature. Jesus' warning is against status-seeking, which applies to Christian teachers as much as to anyone.
47444: "A gifts test will tell me my ministry"
47445: Take a spiritual-gifts inventory, find your top three gifts, and you will know which ministry to join. Your gift profile is your calling.
47446: Paul's lists of gifts vary (Rom 12, 1 Cor 12, Eph 4, 1 Pet 4), suggesting they are examples rather than a complete catalogue. In Scripture people discover their ministry by serving in real needs, being recognised by the community and growing in character, as with the Seven (Acts 6:3) and Timothy (1 Tim 4:14). The Spirit gives gifts "as he wills" and for the common good (1 Cor 12:7-11), and love is the more excellent way (1 Cor 13).
47447: Defenders of inventories, such as many church-growth and small-group trainers, say they are useful starting points that help quiet people name what they enjoy and see their value. Writers such as Thomas Schreiner and Kenneth Berding, while sceptical of fixed lists, accept that reflecting on one's strengths can help. The common ground: tests can prompt reflection but should never replace serving, community confirmation and character.
47448: A test-first approach can make people wait for the perfect fit or refuse needs outside their "gift". A serve-first approach grows gifts through love.
47450: Being a minister means being a humble servant who waits on others; the word diakonos simply means a table waiter.
47451: John N. Collins showed that diakonia language in Greek often refers to a commissioned agent acting on behalf of someone else, a go-between or emissary. Paul is a diakonos of the new covenant (2 Cor 3:6), of God (2 Cor 6:4) and of the gospel (Col 1:23). The point is less the lowliness of the task than the authority of the one who sends.
47452: Others, including many evangelical and Catholic interpreters, agree that Collins corrected an overemphasis but insist that humility remains central, because Jesus explicitly joins diakonia with lowly table service and gives his life as a servant (Luke 22:26-27, Mark 10:45). Both the commissioning and the humility belong together.
47453: If ministry means only lowliness, leaders may neglect real responsibility. If it means only authority, leaders may forget the towel and basin. Jesus models both.
47455: Catholic Church; *Lumen Gentium* (1964), *Apostolicam Actuositatem* (1965), Catechism 871-945 and 1536-1600; theologians Yves Congar, Edward Schillebeeckx
47456: Christ founded his church on the apostles, and bishops succeed them in teaching, sanctifying and governing, with the Pope as successor of Peter. Holy orders has three degrees: bishop, priest and deacon. The ministerial priesthood differs in kind from the common priesthood of the baptised, but both share in Christ's one priesthood. Since Vatican II the church stresses the lay apostolate in the world and lay ministries such as catechist, lector and acolyte.
47457: Strong historical continuity with the early church's bishops; a clear sacramental theology; a rich vision of lay holiness in the world; a worldwide structure that preserves unity.
47458: Protestants argue the New Testament does not support a sacrificing priesthood or a separate clerical caste, and that apostolic succession of office cannot guarantee faithfulness. Some Catholics themselves criticise clericalism. Catholics reply that the succession serves the apostolic faith, not the reverse, and that Vatican II deliberately raised the laity.
47459: Eastern Orthodox churches; John Zizioulas (*Being as Communion*, 1985), Nicholas Afanasiev, Kallistos Ware, Alexander Schmemann
47460: The church is a eucharistic community gathered around its bishop, who is an icon of Christ. Ministries exist within the gathered liturgy: bishop, presbyters, deacons and the laity, who are also an ordained order through baptism and chrismation. Ministry is understood relationally, as a gift within communion rather than a power over others.
47461: Holds ministry and worship together; a deep theology of the whole people of God as the "royal priesthood" in the liturgy; strong continuity with the early church.
47462: Protestants raise the same questions as for Catholic orders. Some Orthodox voices themselves call for fuller lay participation and for recovering the order of deaconesses. Defenders note that Orthodoxy's conciliar and liturgical shape already involves the laity deeply.
47464: John Calvin (*Institutes* 4.3); Westminster Form of Presbyterial Church Government (1645); modern: Timothy Keller, Edmund Clowney
47465: Christ rules his church through his word and through elders. Calvin identified four ongoing offices: pastors, teachers (doctors), elders and deacons. Teaching and ruling elders govern together in sessions, presbyteries and assemblies. All believers share Christ's threefold office and serve God in their vocations.
47466: Plural, accountable leadership; close attention to New Testament patterns; a strong theology of vocation and of the threefold office.
47467: Critics say the distinction between teaching and ruling elders is thin in the text, and that Reformed churches can become dominated by educated clergy. Charismatics say it underplays spiritual gifts. Defenders respond that order and gifts work together, as Paul insists (1 Cor 14:40).
47469: Southern Baptist and other Baptist bodies; congregational churches; Alexander Strauch (*Biblical Eldership*); Mark Dever
47470: Each local congregation is self-governing under Christ. Two offices are recognised, pastor-elder and deacon. The congregation as a whole holds final authority, for example in receiving members and choosing leaders. Strong emphasis falls on the priesthood of all believers and soul liberty.
47471: Takes the local church seriously; gives real responsibility to members; simple structure close to the New Testament's two named offices.
47472: Critics say single-pastor models can concentrate power, independence can isolate churches from accountability, and congregational votes can become political. Many Baptists have responded by recovering plural eldership and voluntary associations.
47474: Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ, many independent churches; Gordon Fee, Amos Yong, Sam Storms, Craig Keener
47475: The Spirit poured out at Pentecost empowers every believer for witness, with gifts including prophecy, healing and tongues. Ministry is charismatic (gift-based) as well as structured. Many Pentecostal bodies ordain women and give large roles to lay evangelists. Most hold that apostolic and prophetic ministries continue in some form, tested by Scripture.
47476: Recovers Acts 2 and Joel 2: every member, including women, the poor and the young, as a Spirit-empowered minister; has driven explosive growth in the Majority World.
47477: Critics warn of weak theological training, celebrity leadership and unchecked prophetic claims. Many Pentecostal scholars agree and call for better discernment and accountability, pointing to Paul's instructions for orderly, tested gifts (1 Cor 14:29-33).
47479: C. Peter Wagner, Bill Hamon and related networks (often called the New Apostolic Reformation); in a different form, Alan Hirsch's APEST
47480: God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet alongside evangelists, pastors and teachers. Apostles provide governing oversight to networks of churches; prophets bring revelation for direction. Hirsch's APEST, by contrast, treats the five as functions every church needs, with no new governing hierarchy.
47481: Takes Ephesians 4 seriously as a description of ongoing ministry; encourages pioneering mission and prophetic courage; explains how many fast-growing independent networks actually function.
47482: Cessationists, many classical Pentecostals (the Assemblies of God formally disapproved the Latter Rain movement's teaching in 1949) and writers such as R. Douglas Geivett and Holly Pivec warn of unaccountable authority, revelation treated as near-scriptural, and political or "dominion" agendas. Supporters reply that abuses are not inherent and that apostles must be accountable. See /movements/dominion-theology and /movements/prophetic-movement.
47484: Schleitheim Confession (1527); Mennonite, Brethren and Hutterite churches; John Howard Yoder (*Body Politics*, 1992); the house-church movement
47485: The church is a community of disciples where everyone has a voice and a role. Leaders are chosen from and by the congregation and remain accountable to it. Discernment is shared (1 Cor 14:29), mutual aid is practised, and ministry is expressed in discipleship, peace-making and service to neighbours.
47486: Embodies the priesthood of all believers; strong accountability; a powerful witness of community, simplicity and peace.
47487: Critics say it can underplay recognised leadership and teaching gifts, and that small, separated communities can become insular. Anabaptists respond that leaders are fully recognised but serve within the community, not above it.
47488: Map the ministries in your church
47489: As a group, list every ministry you can see happening in your church in a month, including hidden ones (cleaning, meals, prayer, giving lifts, counting money).
47490: Sort them using Romans 12:6-8 and 1 Peter 4:10-11 into speaking and serving ministries.
47491: Ask: which needs are not being met? Which gifts are not being used?
47492: Pray together for the people doing hidden ministries, and thank at least one of them this week.
47495: Underline everything about skill and circle everything about character. Count each.
47496: Ask: why does Paul put so much weight on character, home and reputation?
47497: Choose one quality to pray about for yourself this month, whatever your role, and ask a friend to check in with you.
47500: Write down the main tasks of your week, paid or unpaid.
47501: For each, ask: whom does this serve? What part of God's world does it care for? How could I do it more "as for the Lord"?
47502: Share one answer with your group and pray for one another's workplaces by name.
47503: Trace one ministry through the Bible
47504: Choose one: shepherd, priest, prophet, king or hospitality.
47505: Find it in the Old Testament (e.g. Ezek 34, Exod 28, Deut 18, Deut 17, Gen 18).
47506: See how Jesus fulfils or models it (John 10, Heb 7, Luke 4, Matt 21, Luke 14).
47507: See how the church shares it (1 Pet 5, 1 Pet 2, Acts 2, Rev 5, Rom 12). Write one sentence on what it means for you.
47509: Pick one debate from this study: women in ministry, apostles today, or clergy and laity.
47510: Each person reads the strongest case for a view they do not hold, using the Views and Spectrum tabs or a recommended book.
47511: Present it to the group as fairly as its holders would, until they would say, "Yes, that is what we believe."
47512: Then discuss: what did you learn? Where do you still disagree, and how can you serve together anyway?
